young.html: George Eliot was really a woman named Mary Ann Evans. In her time, people did not always take women writers seriously, so she chose a man's name. Her novel Middlemarch is about a whole English town about 200 years ago, and the people in it, all connected like threads in a spider's web.

The main character, Dorothea, wants to do something great and good for the world. Things do not turn out the way she plans. But by the end, she does a great deal of good in quiet ways, helping the people around her. George Eliot says that's how much of the world's goodness happens: through people whose names never make it into history books.

young.html: Unhistoric acts. George Eliot believed small kindnesses add up. For one week, keep a list of small good things you notice people doing: a neighbor helping, a sibling sharing, someone holding a door. At the end, read the list together. How many people did good without anyone noticing?

full.html: Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880) grew up in the English Midlands, the daughter of a land agent. Deeply religious as a girl, she lost her faith in her twenties, translated German works of theology and philosophy, and became an editor of the Westminster Review in London. She took the pen name George Eliot for her novels, beginning in 1857. Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life appeared in eight parts in 1871–72 and is set in 1829–32, the years before the Reform Act of 1832.

items: Dorothea Brooke, ardent and idealistic, marries the elderly scholar Mr. Casaubon, hoping to share in his life's work, a "Key to all Mythologies." She finds him cold, jealous and lost in a project that will never be finished. After his death she gives up his fortune to marry his young cousin, Will Ladislaw.
Tertius Lydgate, a gifted young doctor, comes to town to reform medicine, marries the lovely, self-centered Rosamond Vincy, and is slowly worn down by debt and compromise.
Fred Vincy, Rosamond's idle brother, wins the sensible Mary Garth only after learning honest work from her father Caleb.
Mr. Bulstrode, the pious banker, hides a shameful past that comes back to destroy his standing, and nearly ruins Lydgate too.

full.html: Eliot's narrator often steps back to ask readers to understand even the least likable characters. Of Dorothea weeping on her honeymoon in Rome, she writes:

full.text: If we had a keen vision and feeling of all ordinary human life, it would be like hearing the grass grow and the squirrel's heart beat, and we should die of that roar which lies on the other side of silence. As it is, the quickest of us walk about well wadded with stupidity.
full.author: George Eliot
full.ed: William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh and London

full.html: Eliot believed the novel's great work is to widen our sympathy: to help us feel that every other person has an inner life as real and complicated as our own. Even Casaubon, she insists, has his own "intense consciousness."

full.text: But the effect of her being on those around her was incalculably diffusive: for the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been, is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs.
full.author: George Eliot

full.html: Reading Middlemarch as a story of failure. Most of its people do not achieve their dreams, but the novel honors the quieter good they do, and treats ordinary lives as worthy of the closest attention.

items: Austen, earlier in this era, drew a village; Eliot draws a whole town, with its banks, doctors, politics and gossip.
Aristotle and Kant asked what makes a life good; Eliot's answer is close to Aristotle's practical wisdom, lived among others.
Spinoza, whose Ethics Eliot translated into English (it was published only in 1981), shaped her calm, understanding view of human passions.
Tolstoy, later in this era, shares her belief that history is made by ordinary lives.
Is it better to aim for great deeds or to do small good things well?
How do small choices, like borrowing money or keeping a secret, shape a whole life?
Why is it hard to imagine that other people's inner lives are as real as ours?
What did Eliot mean by "unhistoric acts"?

questions: Dorothea wanted to do something great. What great thing would you like to do? What small good thing could you do this week?
Who in your life does good things quietly, without being noticed?
Why do you think Mary Garth wanted Fred to have a useful job before she married him?
George Eliot used a man's name to be taken seriously. How do you think that felt?
Can you think of someone you didn't like at first and later understood better?
